# Search Params Convention

A filter kept in `useState` is a screen nobody can link to, bookmark, reload or reach with the Back
button — the support conversation about it starts with "click the third tab, then set the date range".
A filter kept in the URL by hand costs the other way: every read re-parses a string, every write
rebuilds a querystring, and the knowledge of which params exist ends up spread across the handlers
that happen to touch them.

nuqs removes both, but only when every screen declares its params the same way. This rule is that way.

## Scope

Applies to **client state that must survive a reload or travel in a link** — table filters, pagination,
sort, the active tab, a selected entity id, a date range — in every hand-written component of an app
that mounts nuqs.

Does **not** apply to:

- Ephemeral UI state nobody would link to — an open modal, a hover, a text input in flight before it is
  committed.
- Server state, which is React Query's ([react-query-convention.md](../react/react-query-convention.md)).
- Route path params, which belong to the router and are read with its own `useParams`.
- A URL built for somewhere else — an external link, a `window.open` target. That is a string, not app
  state.

## The URL is the store

The nuqs adapter is mounted **once**, above the router. From that point nothing else reads or writes the
querystring: no `useSearchParams`, no `URLSearchParams`, and no `useState` holding a copy of a param.

```tsx
// CORRECT — one adapter, above the router
export function RoutesProvider() {
  return (
    <NuqsAdapter>
      <RouterProvider router={router} />
    </NuqsAdapter>
  );
}
```

A `useState` mirror is the failure this rule exists to prevent: two sources for one value, and the one
the user pasted into their address bar is the one that loses.

## One module declares the params

A screen's parsers live in one `{feature}.search-params.ts`, as a single exported object, next to the
serializer built from that same object. A page imports them; it never declares a parser inline, and it
never builds a querystring by hand.

```ts
// CORRECT — routines.search-params.ts
export const routineSearchParams = {
  q: parseAsString.withDefault(''),
  status: parseAsStringEnum(Object.values(RoutineStatusEnum)),
  sortBy: parseAsStringEnum(Object.values(RoutineSortFieldEnum)).withDefault(RoutineSortFieldEnum.NAME),
  page: parseAsInteger.withDefault(1),
  limit: parseAsInteger.withDefault(DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE),
};

export const serializeRoutineSearch = createSerializer(routineSearchParams);

// WRONG — the parser re-declared in the page that uses it
const [page, setPage] = useQueryState('page', parseAsInteger.withDefault(1));

// WRONG — the querystring rebuilt by hand, so the defaults are now known in two places
const params = new URLSearchParams();

if (range.preset !== 'last30days') {
  params.set('range', range.preset);
}
```

The hand-built serializer is the expensive half of that: `createSerializer` already knows every default
and every parser, so it omits what is at its default without being told. A second copy of that knowledge
drifts the first time a default changes.

A group of params several screens share — a date range, a paging window — is a hook of its own,
`use{Thing}SearchParams`, exporting the same object and serializer. The name says search params, not
"query state": `query` is the HTTP querystring DTO ([vocabulary-convention.md](../../core/vocabulary-convention.md#parameters)).

## Related params move together

Params that one user action changes are one `useQueryStates` call and **one** write. `useQueryState` is
for a single param nothing else moves with. Resetting `page` is part of the write that filtered, not a
second statement after it.

```ts
// CORRECT — one read, one write per action
const [search, setSearch] = useQueryStates(routineSearchParams);

const handleOnStatusChange = (status: RoutineStatus | null) => {
  setSearch({ status, page: 1 });
};

const handleOnFilterClear = () => {
  setSearch({ q: '', status: null, type: null, page: 1 });
};

// WRONG — one action, two writes, two renders, and a URL that exists in between
setStatus(value === 'all' ? null : (value as 'active' | 'draft'));
setPage(1);
```

Separate setters also make the intermediate URL real: a filter is applied for one tick while `page`
still points at page 7 of the old result, which is the state the query key is briefly built from.

## An enum param comes from its enum

A param with a closed set of values takes its members from the enum that already declares them
([enum-convention.md](../../core/enum-convention.md)). `parseAsStringEnum` then narrows the value, so a
handler needs no cast.

```ts
// CORRECT — the set is declared once, and the setter is already typed
status: parseAsStringEnum(Object.values(RoutineStatusEnum)),

const handleOnStatusChange = (status: RoutineStatus | null) => {
  setSearch({ status, page: 1 });
};

// WRONG — the union written twice, and the second copy is a cast nothing checks
const [status, setStatus] = useQueryState('status', parseAsStringEnum(['active', 'draft']));

setStatus(value as 'active' | 'draft');
```

## A default, or an absence — never a sentinel

`.withDefault()` belongs on a param the screen always has a value for — `page`, `limit`, `sortBy`. A
filter whose absence means *no filter* gets no default: it reads as `null`, and it is cleared by writing
`null`, which drops the key from the URL.

| Param                              | Declared                        |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| a value the screen always has      | `.withDefault(<value>)`         |
| a filter that may be absent        | no default — `null` when unset  |

Never `''`, `'all'`, `0` or `-1` standing in for "not filtered"
([nullability-convention.md](../../core/nullability-convention.md#never-encode-unknown-as-a-value)) — a
sentinel in a URL is a value the server has to be taught to ignore, in every endpoint that reads it.

Leave `clearOnDefault` alone. Its default drops a param that is at its default value, which is what
keeps the URL short and what makes two identical screens produce the same link.

## The param is the local

The key in the URL and the name bound to it are the same word, and it comes from
[vocabulary-convention.md](../../core/vocabulary-convention.md#parameters): `page`, `limit`, `sortBy`,
`sortOrder`, `q`, `<entity>Id`.

```ts
// CORRECT
const [{ page, limit, sortBy }, setSearch] = useQueryStates(routineSearchParams);

// WRONG — the URL says `interval`, the code says `granularity`, and neither is searchable from the other
const [granularity, setGranularity] = useQueryState('interval', parseAsStringEnum(['daily', 'weekly']));
```

## The options are already right

nuqs's defaults are the correct behaviour for a filter. Change one only for the reason in this table.

| Option            | Leave it, unless                                                                                |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `history`         | the change is navigation the Back button should undo — a tab, a wizard step. A filter is `replace` |
| `limitUrlUpdates` | the write comes from a high-frequency input — `debounce(500)` at that write, and nowhere else     |
| `shallow`         | a server re-reads the params on change — see below                                                |
| `clearOnDefault`  | never                                                                                              |
| `scroll`          | never                                                                                              |

```ts
// CORRECT — the debounce is the write's, so there is still one source for the value
const handleOnKeywordChange = (q: string) => {
  setSearch({ q, page: 1 }, { limitUrlUpdates: debounce(500) });
};

// WRONG — a second copy of `q` in component state, and an external debounce hook around it
const [queryValue, setQueryValue] = useState(keyword);

useDebounce(() => { setKeyword(queryValue); }, 500, [queryValue]);
```

In a framework whose server reads the search params — a route loader, a server component — the params
are read there through `createLoader` / `createSearchParamsCache` built from the **same** parsers object,
and the writes that must reach it pass `shallow: false` with a `startTransition` so the pending render
has a loading state. In a client-only app neither applies and neither is written.

## The URL feeds the query key

The `useQueryStates` object goes straight into the query hook, so the React Query key derives
structurally from the URL and every param change refetches
([react-query-convention.md](../react/react-query-convention.md)). Pass `hasPlaceholder` so paging keeps
the previous rows on screen instead of flashing a spinner.

```ts
// CORRECT
const [search, setSearch] = useQueryStates(routineSearchParams);

const { data: routines, isLoading } = useRoutinesQuery(search, { hasPlaceholder: true });
```

Pagination metadata — total, total pages — comes back in the response and is read from there. Never
recompute it from the URL: the URL says what was asked for, the response says what there is.

## NEVER Do

- Hold a search param in `useState`, or read the querystring through the router, in an app that mounts nuqs.
- Declare a parser inside the component that uses it, or re-declare `page` / `limit` / `sortBy` per screen.
- Build a querystring with `URLSearchParams` where `createSerializer` covers it.
- Write several params with a sequence of single setters — one action is one `useQueryStates` write.
- Pass an inline literal array to `parseAsStringEnum`, or cast a setter's argument to the union it already returns.
- Use `''`, `'all'`, `0` or `-1` for a filter that is simply absent — write `null`.
- Set `clearOnDefault` or `scroll`, or give a filter `history: 'push'`.
- Debounce a nuqs write with an external hook and a mirrored local value.
- Bind a param to a local of a different name.
- Recompute pagination metadata from the URL instead of reading it from the response.
